questions.q: A student writes: "Career and job mean the same thing — both are work you do to earn money." Is this statement correct? Answer yes or no and give the textbook's one-sentence distinction.
questions.a: No. The textbook states: "A career is more than just a job. One may distinguish between a job and a career by saying 'job is an involvement in work for the sake of it' whereas 'a career is driven by a deep desire to excel and a passionate need to grow, develop and prove oneself within the chosen field of work'." A wrong answer reveals the student conflates income-earning with career-building, missing the core motivational and developmental distinction.

questions.q: In the three stone-breakers anecdote, the second man says, "This is my livelihood. I break rocks to make a living in order to feed my family." Explain in your own words how 'livelihood' differs from 'career' using two specific points from the chapter.
questions.a: Livelihood focuses on meeting basic needs and sustaining lifestyle through income from an occupation; it is necessity-driven and present-oriented. Career is a lifelong, dynamic process of progressive achievement driven by personal vision, involving continuous skill upgrading and strategic role transitions for growth and self-actualization. A wrong answer typically equates livelihood with career because both involve work, missing that livelihood is about survival/sustenance while career is about purposeful progression.

questions.q: Riya works as a data entry operator at a BPO. She chose this role because it pays well and allows her to support her family. She has no interest in learning data analytics or moving to a supervisory role. Classify Riya's work engagement as job, livelihood, career, or calling. Justify with two textual evidences.
questions.a: Riya's engagement is a **job** (and also livelihood). Textual evidences: (1) "Work as a job and livelihood: Here work is mainly a source of income enabling desired outcomes; for instance, doing a job to support one's family. The person finds job satisfaction primarily from the income earned." (2) "A career is driven by a deep desire to excel and a passionate need to grow... Such a person gets job satisfaction from continuing advancement and achievements." Riya lacks the desire to excel/grow, so it's not a career. A wrong answer calling it 'career' ignores the absence of progressive achievement motivation.

questions.q: Compare 'work as a calling' and 'work as a career' on three dimensions: (a) source of motivation, (b) role of external rewards (pay, status), (c) relationship to personal identity. Use the textbook's three perspectives (job/livelihood, career, calling) to structure your answer.
questions.a: (a) Calling: inner drives/higher direction; Career: desire to excel and grow professionally. (b) Calling: satisfaction from work itself, external rewards secondary; Career: external rewards (higher posts, status, pay) are milestones of advancement. (c) Calling: work derives from and expresses core identity; Career: identity is built through progressive achievements in a chosen field. A wrong answer blurs calling and career by treating both as 'passionate', missing that calling is intrinsically motivated and identity-expressive, while career is strategically motivated and achievement-oriented.

questions.q: Evaluate this statement: "Since career is a lifelong process, a person who stays in the same government clerical post for 30 years without seeking promotion or skill upgradation has still built a career." Support your evaluation with two arguments from the chapter.
questions.a: The statement is **false**. Argument 1: The chapter defines career as "a field for or pursuit of consecutive progressive achievement" — 'progressive' implies advancement, not stagnation. Argument 2: "It is very important to continually upgrade and learn newer skills, update knowledge and build or enhance competencies, in order to achieve success." A 30-year static role with no skill upgradation lacks the essential career elements of progression and competence-building. A wrong answer accepting the statement confuses 'long tenure' with 'career', ignoring the developmental dimension.

questions.q: Create a realistic 4-sentence mini-case study of a Class 12 student named Arjun who is deciding between two paths after school: (A) joining his father's retail shop immediately for steady income, or (B) pursuing a 3-year design diploma to become a product designer. Label each path as job/livelihood/career/calling and explain Arjun's likely motivation for each in one phrase.
questions.a: Example answer: Arjun's path A (retail shop) is a **job/livelihood** — motivation: "immediate family income". Path B (design diploma) is a **career** — motivation: "progressive creative achievement". A calling version would be: "Arjun feels an inner drive to design sustainable products for rural artisans" — motivation: "inner purpose". A poor answer mislabels path A as 'career' because it's family business, or path B as 'job' because it pays later, showing failure to distinguish income-timing from motivational structure.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Career is a dynamic, lifelong sequence of progressive ______ roles and achievements driven by an individual's deep desire to excel, grow, and actualize their potential within a chosen field, distinct from a job (work performed primarily for income) or occupation (a broad category of similar work roles).

Fill in the blank: ______ you are at a family wedding and your uncle asks, "So, what's your career plan after Class 12?" You hesitate because you're not sure if you want a 'job' for quick money, a 'career' for long-term growth, or something else.
What is Career? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Career is a dynamic, lifelong sequence of progressive professional roles and achievements driven by an individual's deep desire to excel, grow, and actualize their potential within a chosen field, distinct from a job (work performed primarily for income) or occupation (a broad category of similar work roles).

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Career?
questions.a: Students often think 'career' just means 'a good job with promotion prospects' and therefore equate any stable, well-paying, long-term employment with a career.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can clearly distinguish career from job and occupation using three specific differentiating criteria (time horizon, motivation, skill progression), and can analyze a given real-life scenario to classify a person's work engagement as job, livelihood, career, or calling with justification.
